wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e111.summary: Announces the fourth and last principal question of the Prologue: whether theology is practical or speculative.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e127.summary: Lays out the plan for preliminary questions: first, what praxis is (the relation that makes knowledge practical); second, how speculative and practical knowledge differ; third, the main question. It then begins the first.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e138.summary: Poses the first preliminary question: whether only the operation of the sensitive power is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e143.summary: Argument for yes from the Commentator (Eustratius) on Ethics I: 'praxis... is operation according to human choice'. So only operation following choice is praxis. The intellect's operation precedes choice and choice itself is the will's operation, so only the sensitive power's operation follows choice.
claims: Praxis is operation following choice (argument).
Only operations of the sensitive power follow choice (argument).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e160.summary: Argument to the contrary: moral virtue is not acquired without praxis, but moral virtue can exist in the will without any operation of the sensitive power, so praxis can exist without such operation.
claims: Moral virtue can exist in the will without sensitive operation.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e169.summary: Introduces the first of two opinions: only exterior operation, or the operation of a power lower than intellect and will, is praxis.
claims: Only exterior or lower-power operations are praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e178.summary: First argument of that opinion: the practical intellect concerns contingent things we can do, and the work it aims at is necessarily about contingents. All authors take action as passing over to the doable or makeable (agibile, factibile), which are the subjects of the practical intellect and of choice. This is also what distinguishes the active from the contemplative life.
claims: The practical intellect concerns contingent things doable by us (reported).
Action passes over to the doable or makeable (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e196.summary: Second argument: every praxis is operation according to moral virtue, so praxis concerns what choice concerns, namely means to an end and contingent things.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e205.summary: Third argument from Ethics VI.2: the principle of action is choice, and the principles of choice are appetite and reason aimed at an end, namely an action following choice.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e216.summary: Fourth argument from Gregory on Ezekiel ('the virtue of work is beneath the flight of contemplation'): praxis is always beneath contemplation and the intellect's act, and so beneath the will's act, so it is precisely an act of a lower power.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e228.summary: The opinion's account of the right order: the practical intellect investigates what to pursue or avoid; the will chooses the proposed good; and choice is the effective principle of action. After choosing, the will commands the lower powers and the practical intellect to find means and execute. This command, passing into the lower powers and moderating the passions according to moral virtue, is formally praxis and the end of the practical intellect. The will's love of the end is neither action nor making but an operation following speculation. Confirmed by Aristotle: the doable and the choosable are the same.
claims: The will's command passing into the lower powers is formally praxis (reported).
The will's love of the end is not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e278.summary: Ockham argues against the first opinion. Every operation whose directive knowledge is practical, or which is the object of practical knowledge, is praxis. Interior operations are objects of practical knowledge, since practical knowledge is distinguished as being about our operations, those 'whose principle is in the maker' (Metaphysics VI). The principle of interior operations is in us.
claims: Every operation that is the object of practical knowledge is praxis.
Interior operations have their principle in us and are objects of practical knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e311.summary: Further: every act in our power is speculative, practical, or praxis. The will's operation is in our power and is neither speculative nor practical, which are conditions of intellectual acts, so it is praxis.
claims: Every act in our power is speculative, practical, or praxis.
The will's operation is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e322.summary: Introduces the second opinion (Scotus's): praxis is an act of a power other than the intellect, naturally posterior to intellection, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason in order to be right.
claims: Praxis is an act of a non-intellective power, posterior to intellection, apt to conform to right reason (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e331.summary: Defense of the first condition: purely within intellectual acts there is no 'extension' of the intellect, which extends beyond itself only when its act concerns another power's act. That one intellectual act directs another does not make the second praxis or the first practical, or else logic, which directs reasoning, would be practical.
claims: Practical extension requires reference to another power's act (reported).
If intellectual direction of intellectual acts sufficed, logic would be practical (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e351.summary: Defense of the second condition: acts with no order to the intellect (vegetative acts) or naturally preceding intellection (sensing) are not praxes, and practical knowledge does not extend to them insofar as they precede intellection.
claims: Vegetative acts and acts preceding intellection are not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e365.summary: Likewise, acts of the sensitive appetite insofar as they precede intellection are not praxis, since in that way they are shared with brutes. Practical knowledge concerns them only as moderating them, when they follow the moderating intellection.
claims: Sensitive appetite preceding intellection is not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e381.summary: Defense of the third condition from Ethics VI: right choice requires right reason, and likewise every right volition. So every praxis is a volition or follows a volition.
claims: Every right volition requires right reason (reported).
Every praxis is or follows a volition (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e394.summary: Against the first condition: intellection can be praxis. On this doctor's own view, knowledge is practical by extension to praxis as its object. There is practical knowledge of speculation and of acts of understanding, because practical knowledge concerns our works in our power. Intellection is such a work, so it is praxis.
claims: Intellection can be praxis.
There is practical knowledge about acts of speculation.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e416.summary: Further: every operation following choice is praxis, and an act of understanding can follow deliberation and choice, since one can deliberate whether to study and then choose to. Such study is truly praxis.
claims: Study chosen after deliberation is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e436.summary: Further: an intellectual act directing another act through the will is practical, and the directed act is praxis. A dictate that one should study theology at a given place and time directs the act of studying through the will. The reply that this is not extension 'outside itself' only narrows the word's meaning arbitrarily, just as one could restrict 'praxis' to exterior acts, and philosophers use neither restriction. They say only that practical science concerns our works. So any extension to our work as object suffices, and any intellection in our power is praxis or the object of praxis, and not the latter.
claims: A dictate directing study through the will is practical knowledge.
Restricting 'extension' to acts outside the intellect is an arbitrary narrowing.
Any intellection in our power can be praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e493.summary: Answers the objection that then every intellectual habit would be practical, since each extends to an act that is our work. Practical habits extend to our work as an object, while every habit has an act only as elicited by it, not as its object.
claims: Practical habits relate to acts as objects; all habits relate to acts as elicited.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e514.summary: Uses the doctor's own argument that choice of the end is praxis: whatever an appetitive virtue inclines to is praxis, since every such virtue is an elective habit (Ethics III). Appetitive virtue can incline one to study and speculate virtuously at the right place and time, as to pray, so that cognition is praxis.
claims: Appetitive virtue can incline to study and speculation.
Virtuously chosen study is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e538.summary: Further: every act commanded by the will is praxis, and some intellection is commanded by the will just as another power's act is.
claims: Every act commanded by the will is praxis.
Some intellections are commanded by the will.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e545.summary: The doctor's reply: speculation is an operation and so praxis in an extended sense, but in the sense of operations to which the intellect can extend, no intellection is praxis. From 'intellection is commanded by the will' follows 'it is practical', not 'it is praxis': it is named accidentally from the praxis it extends to, but it is not the term of extension.
claims: Speculation is praxis only in an extended sense (reported).
Commanded intellection is practical, not praxis (reported).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e574.summary: Against the reply: intellection is a term of extension, since one intellection dictates that another be elicited. An intellection cannot be morally right unless elicited in conformity with right reason, just as no exterior, sensitive, motive or voluntary act can. If so elicited, it is morally right, so it can truly be praxis.
claims: One intellection can dictate the eliciting of another.
Intellections can be morally right or wrong by conformity to right reason.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e605.summary: Further: 'it is commanded by the will, so it is praxis' does follow. On this doctor's own view, sensitive acts are called praxis only because commanded by the will, so an intellection commanded equally perfectly is equally praxis.
claims: Being commanded by the will makes an act praxis, for intellection as for sensitive acts.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e623.summary: Confirmation: when the commanding act is praxis, the commanded act is also praxis. But 'intellection is commanded, so it is practical' does not follow, since pure speculation, which can in no way be practical, can be commanded by the will.
claims: A commanded act is praxis when the commanding act is.
Pure speculation can be commanded without being practical.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e635.summary: Against the second condition: if it means posterior to an intellection to which it can conform, it is false, since incomplex knowledge alone suffices for praxis, on the doctor's own principles and in truth. If it means that some intellection is presupposed, it is true, since praxis is always a will-elicited or will-commanded act and each presupposes intellection.
claims: Incomplex knowledge alone suffices for praxis.
Every praxis presupposes some intellection.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e653.summary: Against the third condition: some operation is praxis that can in no way be elicited in conformity with right reason, namely one elicited in conformity with the opposite of necessary right reason. There can be a dictate of something impossible, and an act conforming to it, which cannot conform to right reason either to be right or not.
claims: Some praxis cannot be elicited in conformity with right reason.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e673.summary: Confirmation: by parity, an act elicited in conformity with false reason is praxis just as one conforming to right reason is, so not every praxis is apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason.
claims: An act conforming to false reason is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e682.summary: Ockham's own answer begins by saying the difficulty is more verbal than real. Nearly all agree on the sequence: intellection showing the end and means; volition of the end; deliberation about means; a judgment dictating which means to choose; choice; and execution if unimpeded. Example: a sick person's intellect dictates that health is to be sought, the will desires health, the intellect deliberates about walking, potions or remedies, judges one best, the will chooses it, and the act follows. The dispute is only over which of these to call praxis. Since words should be used as authors use them, and Eustratius on the Ethics uses the term most and in accord with Aristotle and Averroes, Ockham will follow his usage.
claims: The dispute about praxis is mostly verbal.
There is broad agreement on the sequence from intellection of the end to execution.
Terms should be used as the authorities use them.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e771.summary: Following Eustratius, distinguishes four senses of praxis: broad, strict, stricter, strictest. Broadly, praxis is the same as energeia, the operation of any power, free or natural. The Commentator says that although praxis and energeia differ in proper meaning, they are used interchangeably, and energeia is the natural power and motion of every substance.
claims: Praxis has four senses: broad, strict, stricter, strictest.
Broadly, praxis equals energeia, the operation of any power.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e808.summary: In the second sense, praxis or energeia is every cognitive operation or passion following on a knower as knower. This includes cognition itself, acts of cognitive and appetitive powers, and passions such as pleasures and sorrows, as well as speaking, walking, eating and drinking, and natural passions like hunger and thirst.
claims: In the second sense, praxis includes cognitive operations, appetitive acts, and passions.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e855.summary: In the third, stricter sense, praxis is operation in our power. Every operation in our power can be virtuous or vicious, and praxis is the work of virtue or vice (Commentator: 'energeia is the work of the virtues', and by the same reasoning the work of vice).
claims: In the stricter sense, praxis is any operation in our power.
Every operation in our power can be virtuous or vicious.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e877.summary: In the strictest sense, praxis is operation elicited in conformity with the dictate of reason and the will's choice, and so with the deliberative intellect, since the deliberable and choosable are the same. Eustratius takes praxis this way: operation according to human choice, where choice judges one alternative over another and is followed by motion and impulse toward the act, then use, the attainment of the end. Doctors discussing whether a science is speculative or practical do not use the first two senses but the third and fourth: the practical intellect extends to praxis in the third sense, and the deliberative intellect always concerns praxis in the fourth.
claims: In the strictest sense, praxis is operation following deliberation and choice.
Debates over practical science concern the third and fourth senses of praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e934.summary: Plans the solution: first, how the practical intellect differs from the deliberative intellect; second, what operation is praxis in the third sense; third, what operation is praxis in the last sense.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e945.summary: On the first point: the practical intellect concerns practical principles and practical conclusions. It concerns the end when it judges that some end is to be desired, which is the first practical principle, so that the end in action is like a principle in speculation. The will does nothing except for an end, dictated by reason or freely set by itself, so every action not about the end presupposes volition of the end. The practical intellect also concerns conclusions, since every truth that agrees with right appetite is practical. The deliberative intellect concerns only practical conclusions: once an end is dictated and willed, it deliberates about the best means and concludes with a determinate one (the sick person and health). So whatever the deliberative intellect concerns, the practical intellect concerns too.
claims: The practical intellect concerns both practical principles about ends and practical conclusions.
The end in action functions like a principle in speculation.
Every voluntary action not about the end presupposes volition of the end.
The will can freely set its own end.
The deliberative intellect concerns only practical conclusions about means.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1028.summary: Clarifies that one and the same intellect is practical, speculative and deliberative. These terms differ only by having distinct nominal definitions. The speculative intellect is the intellect able to consider what is not in our power; the practical intellect is the intellect able to consider or know what is in our power.
claims: One and the same intellect is practical, speculative and deliberative.
These terms differ only in their nominal definitions.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1057.summary: On the second point: every operation in our power is praxis in the third sense. Volition, cognition and exterior acts are all in our power, so each can be called praxis, but praxis is said first of the will's act, since that alone is primarily in our power and nothing else is except through it.
claims: Every operation in our power is praxis in the third sense.
Praxis is said primarily of the will's act, which alone is primarily in our power.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1076.summary: Supports this: every action in our power can be virtuous or vicious, and every such action is praxis. This gives the general description of praxis, which divides into virtuous and vicious praxis, both being in our power.
claims: Praxis divides into virtuous and vicious praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1092.summary: Introduces the description of virtuous praxis (the text is fragmentary here).

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1095.summary: A fragment beginning the definition 'virtuous praxis is...'; the transcription breaks off.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1100.summary: A fragment continuing the definition of virtuous praxis: an operation existing in the will's power, apt to be elicited in conformity (with right reason). The text is garbled in transcription.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1105.summary: Completes the definition (virtuous praxis is an operation in the will's power, apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason in order to be right) and justifies its conditions. No operation outside the will's power is virtuous rather than natural. And per Ethics VI, no right choice, and by parity no right operation, exists without right reason.
claims: Virtuous praxis is an operation in the will's power apt to be elicited in conformity with right reason.
No operation outside the will's power is virtuous.
No right operation is without right reason.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1129.summary: Defines vicious praxis: an operation in the will's power, apt to be elicited contrary to right reason or in conformity with erroneous and false reason. The first condition is needed for imputability, since nothing outside the will's power is imputable. The second holds because every evil act can be dictated not to be chosen.
claims: Vicious praxis is an operation in the will's power elicited contrary to right reason or in conformity with false reason.
Only what is in the will's power is imputable.
Every evil act can be dictated as not to be chosen.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1146.summary: First consequence: not every praxis has a practical science to which it is apt to conform in order to be right. Some bad praxis can never conform to right reason, since no right reason can dictate it, as none can dictate hating an enemy contrary to the divine command.
claims: Not every praxis has a practical science to which it can conform.
No right reason can dictate hatred of an enemy against the divine precept.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1170.summary: Second consequence: some praxis is elicited neither in conformity with nor contrary to right reason, namely one elicited upon the intellect's mere presentation of an object, without any true or false dictate.
claims: Some praxis is neither conformed nor contrary to right reason.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1181.summary: Third consequence: 'praxis' does not signify formally and precisely some act but signifies an act while connoting the will that produces it effectively and freely, as with a meritorious act.
claims: 'Praxis' is a connotative term signifying an act and connoting the will that freely produces it.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1192.summary: From this it follows that the same operation, in species or perhaps in number, can be praxis at one time and not at another. If the will freely and contingently elicits an operation, it is praxis. If God then continued it without any causation or conservation by the will, it would not be praxis, since it would not be in the will's power.
claims: The same operation can be praxis at one time and not at another.
An act conserved by God alone, without the will, is not praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1210.summary: On the third point: praxis in the last sense is every operation in the will's power, deliberated by the intellect, regarding which there is choice. It applies to acts of the will, operations of the intellect, and exterior operations. Given a desire for health as an end, one can deliberate whether health is better gained by exterior operation, by love or hatred, or by intellectual study, since physicians and experience show that each can be a partial cause of sickness or health. So each is deliberable and choosable, and can be praxis in the last sense. Pure speculation can be praxis in this sense. Conversely, an exterior operation commanded by the will is not always praxis in this sense: when set by the will as an end, it is not deliberated or chosen, since we deliberate about means, not ends (Ethics III).
claims: In the last sense, praxis is any operation in the will's power deliberated about and chosen.
Acts of will and intellect can be deliberated and chosen as means.
Pure speculation can be praxis in the strictest sense.
An exterior act willed as an end is not praxis in the strictest sense.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1286.summary: Continues the Aristotelian quotation (Ethics III): the physician does not deliberate whether to heal, the rhetorician whether to persuade, or the statesman whether to make peace. Each posits an end and considers how and by what means to attain it, whether the end comes from right reason or from the will's own setting.
claims: We deliberate about means, not ends.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1298.summary: Qualifies: although not every exterior operation commanded by the will is always praxis in the last sense, it can truly be praxis because it can be ordered to a further end.
claims: An exterior operation can become praxis by being ordered to a further end.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1309.summary: Answers the preliminary question: not only the operation of the sensitive or lower powers is praxis. Operations of intellect and will can also be praxis in the most proper sense.
claims: Operations of intellect and will can be praxis in the most proper sense.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1318.summary: Answers the first opinion's first argument: practical knowledge concerns our works and contingent doables, but it is never said that the praxis or work known practically must be about something contingent or in our power. Only the operation itself must be contingent and doable by us. So pure speculation and love, though their objects are not doable by us, are truly praxes and the objects of practical knowledge.
claims: Praxis need not have a contingent or doable object; the operation itself must be doable.
Pure speculation and love can be praxes.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1342.summary: Objection: all practical knowledge concerns action or making, action is about the doable and making about the makeable, so praxes have contingent objects.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1353.summary: Replies: Aristotle never says practical habits concern action and making, and that these concern doables and makeables. He says practical arts concern the doable and makeable, meaning the action and making themselves (Ethics VI; Eustratius distinguishes practical science, action and making). Many mechanical arts are productive though they concern nothing contingent except the making itself, such as playing the cithara or singing, whose objects are not made by us. So speculation, though about objects not doable by us, can be praxis, since it is itself doable. Aristotle (Ethics I, Metaphysics IX) also notes that some operations leave works behind and some do not, yet both are objects of practical knowledge.
claims: Practical arts concern the action or making itself.
Some practical arts concern nothing contingent except their own operation.
Some operations leave no product and are still objects of practical knowledge.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1414.summary: Quotes the Commentator: when the musician sings or plays an instrument and then stops, no work remains, yet music is truly practical. Nothing there is doable by us except the operation itself, though the instrument is made by another art.
claims: Music is practical though it leaves no product.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1433.summary: Answers the second argument: Ockham concedes that praxis in the strictest sense is operation according to moral virtue and is the subject of choice, and so is contingent and doable by us. But its object need not be contingent. Pure speculation is doable by us, though its object is not, so it can be called praxis but not practical.
claims: Pure speculation can be praxis but not practical.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1453.summary: Answers the objection that moral virtue would then concern intellection and be in the intellect, contrary to Aristotle. Taking moral virtue as any non-intellectual virtuous habit, some moral habit concerns intellection: one can sin by studying at the wrong time and place, or act meritoriously by studying at the right one. Corresponding habits are generated, but moral habits are properly in the will, as Book III will show. Willing to study under due circumstances generates a moral habit in the will, while the commanded intellectual acts generate a separate intellectual habit.
claims: Some moral habits concern intellection.
Studying can be sinful or meritorious depending on circumstances.
All moral habits are properly in the will.
Commanded intellectual acts generate a distinct intellectual habit.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1512.summary: Answers the third argument: choice is always the effective cause of praxis in the strictest sense, and there is choice regarding intellection that is pure speculation, just as regarding exterior operation. So speculation is produced by the will's choice like an exterior act.
claims: Choice can be the effective cause of pure speculation.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1525.summary: Develops this. One can doubt and deliberate whether to consider something purely speculative as one can about eating, conclude that one should, choose to, and the intellection follows choice. Answers Gregory: he takes 'work' for exterior work, as the saints often do, though there is also deliberation about contemplation. Saints deliberate carefully whether to devote themselves to contemplation or to preaching for the sake of eternal life, so contemplation follows choice and is truly praxis. The practical intellect inquires about interior as well as exterior works, so speculation is truly praxis.
claims: One can deliberate and choose whether to speculate.
Gregory's 'work' means exterior work.
Contemplation chosen after deliberation is praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1586.summary: Answers the last authority: since the doable and the choosable are the same, interior operations such as speculation and volition, being doable, are choosable and so truly praxis.
claims: Interior operations are doable and choosable, and so praxis.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1595.summary: Answers the second opinion's first argument: the practical intellect need not extend beyond the whole rational part. It suffices that it extends to the will and to any act through the will's act, so one intellectual act can extend to another as object. Ockham accepts the conclusion that logic would then be practical, to be explained later.
claims: The practical intellect need only extend to the will and acts commanded through it.
Logic is practical.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1614.summary: On the argument for the second condition: it proves only that some intellection precedes every praxis, as it precedes every act of will, not that a dictating or complex intellection is required.
claims: Every praxis is preceded by some intellection, but not necessarily a dictating or complex one.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1630.summary: On the argument for the third condition: conformity to right reason is a condition of good praxis, what Aristotle and the Commentator call eupraxia, not of praxis in general. Every right praxis requires right reason, but not every praxis is or can be right, just as not every volition is.
claims: Conformity to right reason is a condition of eupraxia, not of praxis in general.

wo8uy7-d1e178-d1e1643.summary: Answers the principal argument: only operation following choice is praxis in the fourth sense, but not only lower-power operations follow choice. Intellection and the will's operation do too, since one can deliberate whether to deliberate or to consider. Praxis in the third sense, in relation to which knowledge is called practical, need not follow choice: choice itself and the preceding volition are praxis, being our work and objects of practical knowledge. The Commentator's authority uses the fourth sense. The paragraph ends by announcing another question connected with the fourth principal question.
claims: Intellection and volition can follow choice.
Choice and volition themselves are praxis in the third sense.
One can deliberate about whether to deliberate.

wo8uy7-d1e178.summary: Prologue question 10 opens the fourth principal question (whether theology is practical or speculative) and addresses its first preliminary question: whether only the operation of the sensitive power is praxis. Ockham rejects the opinion that praxis is only the will's command passing into exterior or lower powers, since interior operations have their principle in us and are objects of practical knowledge. He also rejects Scotus's definition of praxis as an act of a non-intellective power, posterior to intellection, apt to conform to right reason. Intellection can be praxis because it can be dictated, deliberated, chosen and commanded; incomplex knowledge suffices for praxis; and acts conforming to false reason are praxis too. Calling the dispute largely verbal, he follows Eustratius's usage: praxis broadly is energeia; then any cognitive or appetitive operation; more strictly any operation in our power; and most strictly operation following deliberation and choice. He distinguishes the practical intellect (principles about ends and conclusions) from the deliberative intellect (conclusions about means), noting that both are one intellect differing in nominal definition. Praxis is primarily the will's act and is a connotative term implying free production by the will, so an act conserved by God alone would cease to be praxis. He defines virtuous and vicious praxis and argues that pure speculation, chosen after deliberation, can be praxis in the strictest sense without being practical knowledge. Logic is practical, and moral habits concerning study reside in the will.
claims: Operations of intellect and will, not only of the sensitive powers, can be praxis.
Praxis is primarily the will's act and connotes free production by the will.
Pure speculation can be praxis without being practical knowledge.
Conformity to right reason belongs to good praxis, not to praxis in general.
The practical and deliberative intellect are one intellect under different nominal definitions.
Logic is practical.
